title: Quorum
summary:
A quorum is **the minimum number of votes that lets a group decide**. For agreement, the quorum is a **majority**: `floor(N/2) + 1` of N nodes.

The whole trick is arithmetic: **any two majorities of the same group overlap in at least one node** (two sets of size > N/2 cannot be disjoint). That shared node has seen both decisions, so two conflicting decisions can never both succeed, and during a network split **at most one side can hold a majority**. Think of a **jury**: a verdict needs a majority, and two different verdicts cannot both have one.

- **Fault tolerance:** a majority quorum survives `f = floor((N-1)/2)` failures, so `N = 2f + 1`: 3 nodes tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2, 7 tolerate 3.
- **Even sizes waste a node:** 4 nodes need 3 votes and still tolerate only 1 failure, and a 2/2 split leaves nobody with a majority.
- **Place nodes with the failure domains in mind:** 3 nodes in one datacenter and 2 in another means losing the big one stops the cluster.

Two flavours share the idea: majority quorums for *agreement* (leader election, [consensus](#/sd/f/consensus), [Raft](#/sd/f/raft)) and tunable `W + R > N` read/write quorums for *replicated data* ([leaderless quorum](#/sd/f/leaderless-quorum), [quorum-based replication](#/sd/f/quorum-based-replication)). The price of a quorum is that without enough live nodes it refuses to answer.

drills.q: A cluster has 7 voting nodes and decisions need a majority. How many votes make a quorum?
drills.explain: A majority is floor(7/2) + 1 = 4. With 3 votes, two disjoint groups of 3 could each decide independently (3 + 3 < 7 leaves one node out); any two groups of 4 must share a node (4 + 4 > 7).

drills.q: You must keep making decisions through 3 simultaneous node failures, using a majority quorum. What is the smallest cluster size?
drills.explain: Survivors must still form a majority: N - 3 >= floor(N/2) + 1 gives N = 7 (4 alive, majority is 4). With N = 6 the majority is 4 but only 3 are alive; with N = 2f + 1 you need 7.

drills.q: Why is a 4-node cluster no better than a 3-node cluster for a majority quorum?
options: Majority of 4 is 3, so both tolerate exactly one failure, and 4 nodes can split 2/2 with no majority on either side
Majority of 4 is 2, so it tolerates two failures but is slower
Four-node clusters cannot elect a leader at all
Quorums are only defined for prime sizes
drills.explain: floor(3/2) = 1 failure for both. The fourth node adds cost and one more way to lose a majority, without adding fault tolerance. Odd sizes are the sweet spot.

drills.q: Five nodes are split by a partition into groups of 3 and 2. A client writes to each side. What does a majority-quorum system do?
options: The 3-node side can commit; the 2-node side cannot reach 3 votes and refuses or stalls
Both sides commit and merge later
Neither side can commit because the cluster is split
The 2-node side commits because it has the original leader
drills.explain: Quorum is how split-brain is avoided: only one side can hold a majority, because 3 + 3 > 5 means two committing groups would have to share a node. The minority side gives up availability to keep consistency.

drills.q: A 5-node cluster has 3 nodes in datacenter A and 2 in datacenter B, with majority quorums. Which failure stops the cluster from making decisions?
options: Datacenter A going offline: only 2 of 5 nodes remain
Datacenter B going offline: 3 of 5 nodes remain
The link between A and B being cut
drills.explain: A holds the majority, so losing A leaves 2 nodes, short of the 3 required. Losing B leaves exactly a quorum, and a cut link leaves A with 3. Two datacenters can never be made symmetric; a quorum across datacenters needs a third site (even a small tiebreaker).

drills.q: State the quorum intersection property and say what it prevents.
drills.answer: Any two majority quorums of the same N nodes share at least one node, since both have more than N/2 members. So two conflicting decisions cannot both be accepted, and in a partition at most one side can proceed, which prevents split-brain. It requires N = 2f + 1 nodes to tolerate f failures.
